Hin Ta and Hin Yai ("Grandfather and Grandmother Rocks") are two naturally eroded granite formations on the shore at the south end of Lamai, shaped by wind and sea into male and female anatomy. Entry is free, parking costs about 20–40 THB, the site is open roughly 08:30–18:30 (Saturday 08:00–19:00), and you reach the rocks through a lane of souvenir and snack stalls. A visit takes 20–45 minutes. Stay off the wet rocks when waves are up, especially October–December.

Map

The rocks are at the southern headland of Lamai Bay, 1–2 km from central Lamai and just off the ring road towards Hua Thanon. The Red Temple (Wat Sila Ngu) is under 1 km away and Overlap Stone about 1.3 km inland.

[kp_places_map area="Lamai" title="Hin Ta and Hin Yai and Lamai"]

The legend

Hin Ta and Hin Yai have a folk tale attached, told in several versions. In a widely told one, an elderly couple sailed from the mainland to Prachuap Khiri Khan to ask for a bride for their son. A storm wrecked their boat as it reached Lamai Bay, both drowned, and their bodies washed ashore and turned into the two rocks, one shaped like a man and one like a woman, as a lasting sign of their journey. Some versions name the couple and the bride's family differently; treat it as local folklore rather than history.

Geologically, the formations are granite boulders weathered by waves, salt and rain into their suggestive shapes. Thai visitors treat the site with good humour, and small offerings are sometimes left on the rocks.

What to expect

From the car park you walk down a short lane lined with stalls to a rocky point with the sea on three sides. Hin Ta, the "grandfather", stands upright among the boulders near the water; Hin Yai, the "grandmother", is a cleft formation lower down on the rock shelf, partly washed by waves. Signs point the way, and on busy days you may queue briefly for a photo.

  • The view looks back north along Lamai Beach and out to the open Gulf.
  • The rock shelf is uneven, with gaps and sharp edges; walk, don't jump between boulders.
  • Climbing on the formations themselves is frowned on by locals and vendors; enjoy them from the paths and lower rocks.
  • Some visitors swim off the rocks on calm days. We don't recommend it: there is no beach entry and the rocks are sharp.

It is a quick, slightly cheeky stop rather than a major sight, and most people combine it with Lamai or the Red Temple.

The stall lane

The lane to the rocks is one of the best places on Samui to buy kalamae, the island's sticky sweet made from glutinous rice flour, palm sugar and coconut cream. You'll also find coconut ice cream served in the shell, fresh coconuts, dried fruit, T-shirts and shell souvenirs.

  • Prices are mostly fixed for snacks; for souvenirs, a little polite bargaining is normal.
  • Many stalls offer tastings of kalamae before you buy.
  • Bring cash in small notes; few stalls take cards.

More on local markets and food: Koh Samui markets.

Wave safety

Hin Ta and Hin Yai sit on the exposed east coast, which takes the full force of the north-east monsoon from October to December. On those days waves break over the lower rocks and the area around Hin Yai can be awash. In November 2024 a visitor was swept off rocks by 2–3 m waves at the Lad Koh viewpoint, a few kilometres up the same coast.

  • When waves are breaking over the lower rocks, stay on the dry upper rocks and take photos from there.
  • Never turn your back on the sea on the rock shelf; sets of bigger waves arrive without warning.
  • Wet, algae-covered rock is very slippery; keep off the dark, wet zone.
  • Watch children closely: there are no railings.

Check sea conditions before you go: [kp_sea_now] More on beach safety and sea conditions.

Children and accessibility

Children usually enjoy the stalls and the scramble, and the subject of the rocks is treated light-heartedly by Thai families. The lane is flat, but the final section is uneven rock with steps and gaps, so it is not suitable for wheelchairs or pushchairs. Carry toddlers on the rocks and keep older children away from the water's edge. See Koh Samui with kids for more family ideas.

Best time to visit

Come before 10:00 or after 16:00: tour minibuses and jungle safaris arrive late morning, and the rocks have little shade at midday, when highs reach 29–33 °C. For calm conditions, February to September is best. In the monsoon months the waves are spectacular from a safe distance. The late-afternoon light is softer for photos, although the sun sets behind you on this east-facing coast.

Visiting respectfully

The rocks are a light-hearted stop, and Thai visitors laugh and pose with them too, but they are also part of local folklore, and small offerings of flowers or incense are sometimes left among the boulders. A few simple rules keep everyone happy:

  • Don't climb on top of Hin Ta or sit on Hin Yai for photos; vendors and guides have objected to visitors doing this.
  • Leave offerings where they are, and don't step over them.
  • Swimwear is fine on the rocks, but cover up in the stall lane and if you go on to the Red Temple afterwards.
  • Take your rubbish back with you: there are few bins on the rocks and plastic ends up in the sea.

A south-east loop

Hin Ta and Hin Yai is easy to combine with the other sights at the southern end of Lamai and the Maret hills. A relaxed half day:

  1. 09:00 Overlap Stone for the view over Lamai before the heat (about 300 THB including a drink).
  2. 10:15 The Red Temple on the ring road below: carved terracotta-red walls, free, 07:00–17:00.
  3. 10:45 Hin Ta and Hin Yai: the rocks, then kalamae and a coconut ice cream in the stall lane.
  4. 11:30 Guan Yu Shrine and the fishing village of Hua Thanon, 2 km south.
  5. 12:30 Lunch, then an afternoon on Lamai Beach.

Prefer waterfalls? Reverse our waterfall and temple day plan, which finishes here at about 17:00.

Is it worth visiting?

Yes, as a short stop if you are in Lamai or passing on the way to the south coast: it is free, close to the road and genuinely quirky, and the stall lane is the best place to try kalamae. It is not worth a long special trip across the island on its own. Expect crowds and a slightly commercial feel at midday, and come early or late for a calmer visit.

Drive south through Lamai towards Hua Thanon and follow the signs to Hin Ta Hin Yai; the lots fill at peak times, so arrive early. Taxis drop visitors at the lane, and Grab works well from Chaweng and Lamai. Songthaews run along the ring road through Lamai in the daytime; agree the fare first. See getting around.
